stem: A 58-year-old man collapses at a gym. You find him unresponsive on his back. Every 8 to 10 seconds he makes a loud, snoring gasp. You check for a carotid pulse and feel none within 10 seconds. Your partner is bringing the AED from the truck. What should you do now?
opts: Insert an oral airway and apply oxygen by nonrebreather mask
Place him in the recovery position and recheck his pulse in 1 minute
Begin chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute
Give two rescue breaths, then recheck the pulse for 10 seconds
key: Occasional gasping (agonal breathing) is not normal breathing; with no pulse, start compressions immediately.
why: Agonal gasps are a sign of cardiac arrest, not effective breathing. A pulseless patient with only gasping needs immediate high-quality compressions, with the AED applied as soon as it arrives.
wrong: Gasping with no pulse is cardiac arrest; oxygen by mask does nothing without circulation and delays compressions.
The recovery position is for a patient who is breathing normally and has a pulse; this patient is in arrest.
The pulse has already been checked; adult CPR begins with compressions once arrest is identified, and a second check only adds delay.

stem: A 71-year-old woman slumps over in a church pew. Members lay her on the floor and tell you she is still breathing. You see her chest move only with an occasional deep gasp. While checking her carotid artery for 10 seconds, you are not sure whether you feel a faint pulse. What is the best action?
opts: Start chest compressions and apply the AED
Keep palpating the carotid pulse until you are certain
Move to the radial artery and check for another 10 seconds
Apply high-flow oxygen and reassess her breathing in 2 minutes
key: If you cannot definitely feel a pulse within 10 seconds in a patient who is not breathing normally, start CPR.
why: Pulse checks are unreliable and must not exceed 10 seconds. A patient with only occasional gasps and no definite pulse is treated as being in cardiac arrest; compressions on a patient who turns out to have a pulse rarely cause serious harm.
wrong: Prolonged pulse checks delay compressions; the limit is 10 seconds.
A radial pulse is harder to feel than a carotid and extends the delay without changing the decision.
Gasping is not normal breathing; waiting 2 minutes on oxygen leaves a possibly pulseless patient without circulation.

stem: Lifeguards pull a 30-year-old man from a pool onto the deck. He is unresponsive and pulseless, and your partner starts compressions. His chest is wet. The AED is ready. What should you do?
opts: Delay defibrillation until he is moved indoors and completely dried
Quickly wipe his chest dry, then apply the pads and analyze
Apply the pads directly over the wet skin to avoid any delay
Withhold the AED because water makes defibrillation unsafe for rescuers
key: A wet chest is wiped dry quickly before pad placement; water is not a reason to withhold or delay the AED.
why: Water on the chest can reduce pad adhesion and let current travel across the skin instead of through the heart. A quick wipe takes seconds; the patient does not need to be fully dried or moved indoors once he is out of the water and no one touches him during the shock.
wrong: Moving and fully drying the patient wastes minutes when only the chest needs to be wiped.
Water on the chest can reduce pad adhesion and divert current; wiping it first takes only seconds.
An AED can be used once the patient is out of the water and the chest is dried; withholding it removes his best chance.

stem: A 66-year-old man is in cardiac arrest in his kitchen. When you expose his chest, you see a firm, coin-sized bulge under the skin just below his right collarbone, exactly where the upper AED pad normally goes. What is the correct approach?
opts: Skip the AED because the implanted device will treat the rhythm
Place the upper pad directly over the bulge to ensure good contact
Do CPR only, because a shock could damage the implanted device
Place the pad off the device and analyze without delay
key: Avoid placing an AED pad directly over an implanted pacemaker or defibrillator, but do not delay defibrillation.
why: A pad directly over an implanted device can block or divert current. Shifting the pad so it is not over the device, or using front-to-back placement, keeps current flowing through the heart without delaying the shock.
wrong: An implanted device may have failed or be unable to correct the rhythm; the AED must still be used.
A pad directly over the device can impede current delivery to the heart.
Concern for the device never outweighs the need to defibrillate a shockable rhythm.

stem: An 80-year-old woman in cardiac arrest has a medication patch on her right upper chest, exactly where the AED pad should go. Your partner is doing compressions. What should you do before applying that pad?
opts: Remove the patch, wipe the skin, then apply the pad
Apply the pad on top of the patch to save time
Place both pads on her back to avoid the patch
Leave the patch and skip defibrillation until ALS arrives
key: Remove a medication patch and wipe the skin before placing an AED pad over that area.
why: A patch under the pad can block current delivery and cause a skin burn. Removing it with gloves and wiping the area takes only seconds and does not meaningfully delay the shock.
wrong: A pad over a patch can block current delivery and may burn the skin.
Both pads on the back will not direct current through the heart.
The patch is easily removed; skipping defibrillation removes her best chance of survival.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is found unresponsive and pulseless at a daycare. CPR is in progress. Your AED kit has only adult pads, and there is no pediatric attenuator. What should you do?
opts: Withhold the AED and continue CPR until ALS arrives with pediatric equipment
Use the adult pads, placing them so they do not touch, front-to-back if needed
Cut the adult pads in half so they fit the child's chest
Place both adult pads side by side on the front of the chest, overlapping if needed
key: Use pediatric pads or an attenuator if available; otherwise use adult pads that do not touch, front-to-back on a small chest.
why: Defibrillation of a shockable rhythm is more important than the dose reduction pediatric equipment provides. Adult pads are used when nothing else is available, as long as they do not touch; front-to-back placement makes room on a small chest.
wrong: If pediatric pads or an attenuator are unavailable, adult pads are used rather than withholding defibrillation.
Cutting pads damages them and makes current delivery unpredictable.
Touching or overlapping pads let current arc across the chest instead of through the heart.

stem: You and your partner are performing CPR on a 7-month-old infant in cardiac arrest. Your partner is giving breaths with a bag-valve mask while you compress. Which compression technique and ratio should you use?
opts: Two fingers on the lower sternum, 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Two-thumb encircling hands, 30 compressions to 2 breaths
Two-thumb encircling hands, 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Heel of one hand, 30 compressions to 2 breaths
key: Two-rescuer infant CPR uses 15:2; compress with two-thumb encircling or heel of one hand, not two fingers (2025).
why: With two rescuers, infants and children receive 15 compressions to 2 breaths. The 2025 guidelines recommend the two-thumb encircling technique or the heel of one hand because the two-finger technique often fails to reach adequate depth.
wrong: The 2025 guidelines no longer recommend the two-finger technique; it produces shallower compressions.
30:2 is the single-rescuer ratio; two rescuers use 15:2 for infants and children.
30:2 is the single-rescuer ratio; with two rescuers the infant ratio is 15:2.

stem: Off duty and alone, you find a 3-month-old infant unresponsive, not breathing, and with no brachial pulse. You call 911 on speakerphone and begin CPR. Which ratio and compression depth are correct?
opts: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, about 1.5 inches (one-third of chest depth)
15 compressions to 2 breaths, about 1.5 inches (one-third of chest depth)
30 compressions to 2 breaths, about 2.5 inches deep
15 compressions to 2 breaths, about 1 inch deep
key: Single-rescuer infant CPR is 30:2 with compressions about 1.5 in (4 cm), one-third of the chest depth.
why: A lone rescuer uses 30:2 for all ages. Infant compressions should be at least one-third of the front-to-back chest depth, about 1.5 inches.
wrong: 15:2 is used only when two rescuers are present.
2.5 inches is deeper than recommended for an infant and risks injury.
15:2 is for two rescuers, and 1 inch is shallower than one-third of the chest depth.

stem: You are reviewing CPR calls from the past month. No advanced airway was in place on any of them. Classify the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio for each situation.
rows: One EMT alone with a 50-year-old adult
One EMT alone with a 9-month-old infant
key: Adults are 30:2 regardless of rescuer number; children and infants are 30:2 with one rescuer and 15:2 with two.
why: The adult ratio stays 30:2 with any number of rescuers. For children and infants, a second rescuer allows 15:2, which delivers more ventilations because pediatric arrest is often caused by respiratory failure.

stem: You and a firefighter are doing two-rescuer CPR on a 62-year-old woman with an AED attached. You have been compressing for about 2 minutes, you feel fine, and your compressions still look deep. The AED is about to analyze. What should happen?
opts: Keep compressing because you are not yet fatigued
Switch only when your compressions visibly become shallow
Switch compressors every 5 minutes to limit interruptions
Switch compressors during the analysis, in under 5 seconds
key: Change compressors about every 2 minutes, ideally during rhythm analysis, with the switch done in under 5 seconds.
why: Compression quality declines within about 2 minutes, often before the rescuer notices fatigue. Swapping during the AED analysis uses a pause that already exists and keeps interruptions short.
wrong: Rescuers fatigue before they notice it; compressors should switch about every 2 minutes regardless.
Compression quality declines before fatigue is visible; waiting allows poor compressions.
Five minutes is too long; quality drops within about 2 minutes.

stem: You and your partner arrive at a witnessed collapse of a 60-year-old man in a hardware store. Put your actions in the correct order.
opts: Confirm the scene is safe and the patient is unresponsive
Check for normal breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds
Begin chest compressions while your partner applies the AED pads
Stop compressions and clear the patient when the AED analyzes
Deliver the shock with no one touching the patient
Immediately resume compressions for about 2 minutes before the next analysis
key: After a shock, compressions resume immediately; there is no pulse check until the next 2-minute analysis.
why: Compressions start as soon as arrest is identified and continue while the AED is applied. After the shock, compressions restart at once because the heart rarely produces an effective pulse immediately, and any pause reduces blood flow.

stem: A 79-year-old man is pulseless and apneic on his bedroom floor. He is warm, with no rigor mortis or dependent lividity. His daughter says he has terminal lung cancer and 'would not want this,' but no DNR order or POLST form can be found. What should you do?
opts: Withhold CPR because the daughter has stated his wishes
Begin CPR with the AED and contact medical direction
Start CPR only if the daughter gives permission
Call the medical examiner and document the time of death
key: Without a valid DNR or obvious signs of death, begin resuscitation; stopping is a medical direction or protocol decision.
why: A family member's verbal report is not a valid advance directive. With no documentation and no obvious signs of death, the EMT starts resuscitation and involves medical direction, who can help weigh the family's information.
wrong: A verbal report from family is not a valid advance directive; without documentation, resuscitation is started.
Without valid documentation, starting resuscitation does not depend on family permission; begin care and involve medical direction.
No obvious signs of death are present, so declaring death is not an EMT decision here.

stem: You and your partner have done 20 minutes of high-quality CPR on a 55-year-old man. The AED has advised no shock at every analysis, and ALS is 10 minutes away. Your partner says it is time to stop. Your protocols do not authorize EMTs to terminate resuscitation on their own. What should you do?
opts: Stop CPR and record the time, since the rhythm is not shockable
Stop CPR only if family members agree it is time
Continue CPR and contact medical direction for guidance
Stop compressions but continue ventilations until ALS arrives
key: Terminating resuscitation is not an EMT's own decision; continue CPR and follow protocol or online medical direction.
why: A non-shockable rhythm does not by itself authorize an EMT to stop. Unless a protocol allows it, resuscitation continues while medical direction is contacted for a termination decision.
wrong: A no-shock rhythm alone does not authorize an EMT to stop; termination requires protocol or medical direction.
Family agreement does not give the EMT authority to terminate resuscitation.
Ventilation without compressions provides no circulation and still amounts to stopping resuscitation.

stem: You are coaching a new EMT who is doing compressions on an adult in cardiac arrest. Which actions reflect high-quality CPR? Select THREE.
opts: Compressing at 100 to 120 per minute
Pushing at least 2 inches but not more than 2.4 inches deep
Allowing the chest to fully recoil after each compression
Pausing every 30 seconds to check for a carotid pulse
Leaning on the chest between compressions to keep the hands in place
Compressing at about 150 per minute to increase blood flow
key: High-quality adult CPR: 100–120/min, 2–2.4 in deep, full recoil, and minimal interruptions.
why: Correct rate, correct depth, and full recoil together produce the best blood flow during CPR. Pauses, leaning, and excessive rates all reduce the effectiveness of compressions.
wrong: Frequent pulse checks interrupt compressions; pauses should be minimized and pulse checks wait for rhythm analysis.
Leaning prevents full recoil and reduces filling of the heart between compressions.
Rates above 120 per minute reduce compression depth and filling time.

stem: A 40-year-old man cut his forearm on a broken window. Dark red blood flows steadily from a 3-inch laceration but is not spurting or pooling. He is alert, and his skin is warm and pink. What is the first step to control the bleeding?
opts: Apply a tourniquet high on the upper arm
Apply firm direct pressure with a dressing over the wound
Pack the wound with gauze before applying pressure
Elevate the arm and wait to see if the bleeding slows
key: Steady bleeding that is not life-threatening is controlled first with firm direct pressure.
why: Direct pressure controls most external bleeding. This wound is not spurting or pooling and the patient is perfusing well, so a tourniquet or packing is not needed unless pressure fails.
wrong: A tourniquet is for life-threatening extremity bleeding or bleeding that direct pressure cannot control.
Packing is for deep wounds where surface pressure cannot reach the bleeding source, such as junctional wounds; this laceration responds to direct pressure.
Elevation alone is not an effective bleeding control method and delays direct pressure.

stem: A 25-year-old landscaper slipped with a chainsaw. Bright red blood is spurting from a deep wound in the middle of his right thigh, and a large pool is forming on the ground. He is pale and anxious. What should you do first?
opts: Obtain a full set of vital signs to establish a baseline
Apply direct pressure and reassess after 10 minutes
Apply a pressure bandage and elevate the leg
Apply a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound
key: Spurting or pooling extremity bleeding is life-threatening: apply a tourniquet 2–3 in proximal to the wound immediately.
why: Massive extremity hemorrhage can be fatal within minutes, so it is controlled before vital signs or further assessment. A tourniquet placed 2 to 3 inches above the wound, avoiding a joint, is the fastest reliable control.
wrong: Vital signs can wait; uncontrolled arterial bleeding can kill him within minutes.
Waiting 10 minutes with spurting, pooling bleeding risks fatal blood loss; a tourniquet is indicated now.
A pressure bandage is unlikely to control arterial bleeding of this size, and elevation adds little.

stem: You applied a tourniquet 3 inches above a deep lower-thigh wound on a 34-year-old man and tightened the windlass until it would not turn further without great force. Blood is still flowing briskly from the wound. What should you do next?
opts: Apply a second tourniquet just above the first
Remove the first tourniquet and reapply it lower
Loosen the tourniquet and switch to direct pressure
Pack the thigh wound and remove the tourniquet
key: If a fully tightened tourniquet does not stop bleeding, apply a second tourniquet proximal to the first.
why: A large thigh may need more compression than one tourniquet can deliver. Leaving the first in place and adding a second just above it increases the compressed area without allowing more blood loss.
wrong: Removing it allows more bleeding, and placing it lower moves it closer to the wound.
Loosening restores flow to the wound and allows further blood loss.
Removing a tourniquet that is partly working causes more bleeding; add a second one instead.

stem: Fifteen minutes ago you applied a tourniquet that stopped severe bleeding from a 50-year-old woman's lower leg. She is now crying from pain at the tourniquet site and begs you to loosen it. Transport to the trauma center will take 25 more minutes. What should you do?
opts: Loosen it for 1 minute every 10 minutes to restore circulation
Remove it and apply a pressure dressing, since the bleeding has stopped
Leave it in place, reassure her, and record the application time
Loosen it slightly until she can tolerate the pain
key: Once applied, a tourniquet is not loosened or removed in the field; document the time and reassure the patient.
why: Pain is expected with an effective tourniquet. Loosening or removing it risks renewed bleeding, so it stays in place and the time of application is documented for the receiving team.
wrong: Periodic loosening causes repeated blood loss and is not recommended.
Removing a tourniquet in the field risks rebleeding; removal is a hospital decision.
Partial loosening can let arterial bleeding resume while blocking venous return, worsening blood loss.

stem: A 19-year-old man was stabbed in the left groin crease. Bright red blood is pouring from a deep 1-inch wound. He is pale and restless, HR 128. There is no room to place a tourniquet above the wound. What is the best method to control this bleeding?
opts: Apply a tourniquet as high on the thigh as it will go
Pack the wound with gauze and hold firm pressure
Cover the wound with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides
Apply ice packs to the groin and elevate the legs
key: Junctional wounds (groin, armpit, neck) that cannot take a tourniquet are packed with gauze and held with firm pressure.
why: Packing places gauze directly against the bleeding vessel deep in the wound, and firm pressure on top compresses it. A tourniquet cannot be placed above a groin crease wound.
wrong: A thigh tourniquet sits below a groin crease wound and cannot compress the bleeding vessel.
An occlusive dressing is for open chest wounds and does not control junctional hemorrhage.
Cold and elevation do not control arterial bleeding from a deep wound.

stem: A 45-year-old man was struck by flying glass and has a deep wound in his right armpit. Blood is flowing heavily and has soaked through two stacked trauma dressings under your hand. What should you do next?
opts: Apply a tourniquet on the upper arm below the wound
Add more dressings on top and continue the same pressure
Apply a cold pack and raise the arm above his head
Pack gauze into the wound and hold firm pressure
key: Heavy bleeding from a deep armpit wound is controlled by packing the wound and holding firm pressure, not by a limb tourniquet.
why: The armpit is a junctional area where a tourniquet cannot be placed above the wound. Packing puts pressure on the bleeding source inside the wound, which stacked surface dressings cannot do.
wrong: A tourniquet on the arm is below an armpit wound and will not control it.
Stacking dressings on the surface of a deep wound does not press on the bleeding source inside it.
Cold and elevation do not control heavy bleeding from a deep wound.

stem: You arrive at a multi-vehicle crash with several bleeding patients. Which findings indicate life-threatening bleeding that needs immediate control? Select THREE.
opts: Blood spurting from a wound on a patient's upper arm
Blood pooling on the pavement under a patient's leg
Blood soaking through a dressing that is already being pressed on a wound
A scraped forearm with slow oozing that stopped with light pressure
A small scalp laceration that bled briefly and is now controlled
A shin skin tear with a slow trickle of dark blood
key: Spurting blood, pooling blood, or bleeding that soaks through applied pressure is life-threatening.
why: These signs show rapid blood loss that can cause shock and death within minutes and must be controlled during the primary assessment. Slow oozing or bleeding already controlled can wait.
wrong: Slow oozing that stops with light pressure is not life-threatening.
A scalp wound that is already controlled does not need immediate intervention.
A slow trickle of dark blood is minor venous or capillary bleeding.

stem: You are directing bleeding control for several injured workers after an industrial accident. Classify the most appropriate primary bleeding-control method for each patient.
rows: Steady dark bleeding from a forearm laceration that slows under your hand
Deep, heavily bleeding wound in the groin crease
Spurting wound on the lower leg with blood pooling
Deep, heavily bleeding wound in the armpit
Upper-arm laceration that keeps soaking through firm direct pressure
key: Direct pressure for controllable bleeding, tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding, packing for junctional wounds.
why: Bleeding control matches the wound location and severity. Limb wounds that are life-threatening or fail direct pressure get a tourniquet, while groin and armpit wounds, where a tourniquet cannot be placed, are packed.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has spurting, pooling bleeding from a deep wound in the middle of her upper arm. Put the steps of tourniquet application in the correct order.
opts: Expose the wound and identify the bleeding site
Place the tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Pull the strap as tight as possible and secure it
Twist the windlass until the bleeding stops
Lock the windlass in place
Record the time the tourniquet was applied
key: Tourniquet: place 2–3 in proximal, tighten the strap, twist the windlass until bleeding stops, lock it, and note the time.
why: Removing slack with the strap before twisting lets the windlass reach occlusion with fewer turns. Locking keeps it from unwinding, and the recorded time guides hospital care.

stem: A 34-year-old man was the driver in a moderate-speed crash. He is anxious and keeps asking what happened. His skin is pale, cool, and moist. HR 118, BP 124/82, RR 22, SpO2 97%. Capillary refill is about 3 seconds. His abdomen is tender and distended. How should you interpret his condition?
opts: Compensated shock, likely internal bleeding; high priority
Normal stress response, since his blood pressure is normal
Decompensated shock, since his heart rate is above 100
Anxiety reaction; reassess vital signs after calming him
key: Tachycardia, cool pale moist skin, and anxiety with a normal BP indicate compensated shock.
why: The body keeps blood pressure normal early in shock by raising the heart rate and shunting blood away from the skin. His abdominal findings suggest internal bleeding, which needs rapid transport.
wrong: A normal BP does not rule out shock; tachycardia, cool moist skin, and delayed refill show compensation.
Decompensation is marked by falling blood pressure, which has not occurred yet.
Attributing these signs to anxiety risks missing hemorrhage; the abdominal findings point to internal bleeding.

stem: You are transporting a 45-year-old woman with a pelvic injury. On scene her HR was 112 and BP 128/84. Twenty minutes later she is confused, HR 136, BP 82/50, and her skin is gray and clammy. What does this change indicate?
opts: Improvement, since compensation is no longer needed
An expected effect of pain; continue routine monitoring
Progression to decompensated shock, a late and ominous sign
A measurement error; recheck with a larger cuff before acting
key: A falling blood pressure with worsening mental status marks decompensated shock, a late sign.
why: Hypotension appears when the body can no longer compensate for blood loss. Together with new confusion and gray skin, it shows she is deteriorating and needs urgent care and hospital notification.
wrong: Falling BP means compensation is failing, not that it is no longer needed.
Pain does not explain hypotension, confusion, and gray skin together.
The reading matches her worsening mental status and skin; delaying action to recheck is dangerous.

stem: A 5-year-old boy has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. He is listless and barely looks at you. HR 162, RR 30, BP 98/60, which is normal for his age. His hands and feet are cool and mottled, and capillary refill is 4 seconds. What is the best interpretation?
opts: He is not in shock because his blood pressure is normal for his age
Compensated shock; low blood pressure is a late sign in children
His fast heart rate is from fever and anxiety, so shock is unlikely
He is in shock only if his blood pressure falls below 70 mm Hg
key: Children keep a normal BP until late in shock; tachycardia, poor perfusion, and altered mental status come first.
why: Children compensate strongly with heart rate and vasoconstriction, so blood pressure stays normal until they are close to collapse. Listlessness, mottling, and slow capillary refill show shock now.
wrong: Children maintain blood pressure until late; tachycardia, mottling, and slow refill already show shock.
A listless child with mottled skin and slow refill has a perfusion problem, not simple anxiety.
Waiting for hypotension in a child means waiting for decompensation and impending arrest.

stem: A 78-year-old woman fell down several stairs and has a deformed, swollen thigh. She takes metoprolol and says her blood pressure is 'usually around 150.' She is pale and cool. HR 72, BP 104/68, RR 20. Why is a heart rate of 72 not reassuring?
opts: A heart rate of 72 confirms that her blood loss is minor
Pain from the fracture is lowering her heart rate
Femur fractures slow the heart by stimulating the vagus nerve
Her beta-blocker can blunt the tachycardia of shock
key: Beta-blockers can mask tachycardia; in older adults, judge shock by perfusion and baseline BP, not heart rate alone.
why: Metoprolol blunts the heart rate response to blood loss. Her pale, cool skin and a BP far below her usual baseline suggest significant bleeding into the thigh despite a normal-looking pulse.
wrong: Beta-blockers blunt the heart rate response, so a normal rate cannot rule out significant bleeding.
Pain usually raises heart rate; it does not explain a lack of tachycardia.
Femur fractures do not slow the heart; they can cause major blood loss into the thigh.

stem: An 81-year-old man has had black, tarry stools for 2 days and nearly fainted getting out of bed. He takes atenolol for high blood pressure. He is pale, sweaty, and anxious. HR 66, BP 96/58, RR 22. His wife says his usual BP is about 140/80. How should you manage this patient?
opts: As a high-priority patient in shock from likely GI bleeding
As stable, since his heart rate is normal
As a simple fainting episode after standing too fast
As low priority unless his heart rate rises above 100
key: In a beta-blocked patient, relative hypotension and poor perfusion signal shock even when heart rate is normal.
why: Tarry stools suggest upper GI bleeding. His beta-blocker can keep his pulse near normal, so the drop from his usual BP, pale sweaty skin, and near-fainting are the real signs of shock.
wrong: His beta-blocker can blunt tachycardia; pale, sweaty skin and a BP well below baseline indicate shock.
Near-fainting with tarry stools and poor perfusion points to blood loss, not a harmless faint.
A beta-blocked patient may never become tachycardic; waiting for HR above 100 delays care.

stem: A 29-year-old woman ate a cookie containing peanuts 10 minutes ago. She has hives on her chest and arms, feels lightheaded, and her skin is warm and flushed. HR 124, BP 78/44, RR 24 with faint wheezes. She carries a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. What is the best interpretation and action?
opts: Hypovolemic shock; lay her flat and wait for ALS before giving any medication
Panic attack; coach her breathing and recheck vital signs
Anaphylactic (distributive) shock; administer her epinephrine auto-injector
Mild allergic reaction; give oral fluids and monitor during transport
key: Hives, warm flushed skin, and hypotension after allergen exposure indicate anaphylactic (distributive) shock: give epinephrine.
why: Anaphylaxis dilates blood vessels and causes leaky capillaries, producing distributive shock. Epinephrine is the first-line treatment and should not be delayed.
wrong: There is no fluid loss; this is allergic distributive shock, and epinephrine should not wait for ALS.
Hives, hypotension, and wheezing after a known allergen exposure are anaphylaxis, not panic.
Hypotension and wheezing make this anaphylaxis, not a mild reaction, and oral intake is unsafe.

stem: A 67-year-old man has had crushing chest pain for an hour. He is pale, cool, and sweaty. HR 112, BP 84/56, RR 28, SpO2 89%. You hear crackles in both lower lungs, and his neck veins are distended while he sits upright. Which type of shock is most likely?
opts: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Distributive shock
Neurogenic shock
key: Chest pain with hypotension, crackles, and distended neck veins suggests cardiogenic shock from pump failure.
why: When the heart fails as a pump, blood backs up into the lungs (crackles) and the veins (distended neck veins) while output falls. Hypovolemic and distributive shock do not cause this backup.
wrong: Hypovolemic shock causes flat neck veins and clear lungs, not crackles and distended neck veins.
Distributive shock usually has warm, flushed skin and lacks signs of fluid backing up into the lungs.
Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury and typically has warm skin and a slow heart rate.

stem: You sealed a stab wound to a 31-year-old man's right chest with an occlusive dressing taped on all four sides. Ten minutes later he is increasingly short of breath and anxious. HR 134, BP 78/50, his neck veins are distended, and breath sounds are absent on the right. ALS is 15 minutes away. What should you do?
opts: Add a second occlusive dressing over the first
Lay him supine with his legs raised and continue transport unchanged
Insert a needle into the right chest to release the trapped air
Briefly lift one edge of the dressing to let air escape, then reseal
key: Signs of tension pneumothorax after an occlusive dressing: briefly lift the dressing to let air escape.
why: Air trapped in the chest is compressing the heart and great vessels, causing obstructive shock. Lifting the dressing lets the trapped air escape, which is within EMT scope; needle decompression is not.
wrong: Another seal traps more air and worsens the tension pneumothorax.
Positioning does not relieve trapped air; this obstructive shock needs the pressure released.
Needle decompression is outside EMT scope.

stem: A 22-year-old man has a deep leg laceration with heavy bleeding that you have just controlled. You are watching for signs that he is developing shock. Which findings are early signs of shock? Select TWO.
opts: Restlessness or anxiety
Rising heart rate
Falling systolic blood pressure
Fixed, dilated pupils
Slowing heart rate
key: Anxiety and tachycardia are early shock signs; hypotension is a late sign.
why: Early in shock, reduced blood flow to the brain causes restlessness, and the heart speeds up to maintain output. Blood pressure falls only when compensation fails.
wrong: Falling blood pressure is a late sign that compensation is failing.
Fixed, dilated pupils are a very late finding near death.
A slowing heart rate in shock usually occurs late, just before arrest.

stem: You are reviewing five patients transported in shock. Classify each patient's most likely type of shock.
rows: Pale, cool skin and a rapid pulse after a femur fracture
Warm, flushed skin, hives, and low BP after a bee sting
Chest pain, crackles in both lungs, and low BP
Penetrating chest wound, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on one side, and low BP
Fever, warm skin, confusion, and low BP in a patient with pneumonia
key: Shock type is recognized by cause and findings: volume loss, vessel dilation, pump failure, or mechanical obstruction.
why: Hypovolemic shock follows fluid or blood loss; anaphylaxis and sepsis are distributive; pump failure is cardiogenic; tension pneumothorax blocks blood return and is obstructive.

stem: At 0730 a man calls because his 69-year-old wife cannot lift her right arm and her speech is garbled. He noticed it when she woke up at 0700. She was normal when they went to bed at 2300. What time should you report as last known well?
opts: 2300, when she was last seen normal
0700, when the symptoms were discovered
0730, when the call was placed
The time your unit arrived on scene
key: Last known well is the last time the patient was seen at baseline, not when symptoms were found.
why: Hospital stroke treatment choices depend on how long symptoms may have been present. For a patient who wakes with symptoms, the clock starts when she was last seen normal.
wrong: 0700 is when symptoms were discovered, not when she was last seen normal.
0730 is the time of the call, not the last time she was normal.
Arrival time has no relation to when the stroke began.

stem: A 74-year-old man at a shopping mall has a sudden left-sided facial droop and left arm drift. His airway is clear and breathing is adequate. His adult son was with him all morning. Before you leave the scene, which information from the son is most important to obtain?
opts: The name of the man's primary care physician
When the son last saw his father acting normally
Whether the man had similar symptoms several years ago
The man's health insurance company and policy number
key: For suspected stroke, get the last known well time from a witness before leaving the scene.
why: Eligibility for time-sensitive stroke treatment depends on the last known well time. A witness may not be available at the hospital, so it must be obtained on scene.
wrong: Useful later, but it does not affect time-sensitive stroke treatment.
Past history helps the hospital but does not drive time-critical treatment decisions like last known well does.
Insurance has no bearing on prehospital stroke care.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes calls because she feels 'wiped out' and nauseated and became short of breath carrying laundry upstairs. She denies chest pain. She is pale and slightly sweaty. HR 98, BP 146/88, RR 20, SpO2 96%. What is the best approach?
opts: Treat as a likely viral illness and suggest she follow up with her doctor
Treat as low blood sugar and give oral glucose before checking her level
Treat as possible acute coronary syndrome; transport promptly, ALS per protocol
Treat as anxiety and coach slow breathing before deciding on transport
key: Women, diabetics, and older adults often have ACS without chest pain: fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, or sweating.
why: Her age, sex, diabetes, and exertional symptoms with pale, sweaty skin fit an atypical ACS presentation. She needs prompt transport and an ECG, which ALS or the hospital can obtain.
wrong: Fatigue, nausea, and exertional shortness of breath in an older diabetic woman can be ACS; dismissing it risks a missed heart attack.
Glucose should be measured before treating, and her presentation is more concerning for ACS.
Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion; these symptoms require evaluation for ACS.

stem: An 82-year-old man says he has 'indigestion' in his upper abdomen that began 40 minutes ago while he was shoveling snow. He also feels weak and lightheaded and is sweating heavily. HR 54, BP 102/64, RR 20, SpO2 95%. He asks you to just bring him an antacid. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Give him the antacid and advise him to rest indoors
Have him walk to the ambulance to see whether symptoms worsen with exertion
Wait 15 minutes to see whether the discomfort settles
Treat as possible acute coronary syndrome, request ALS, and transport
key: Exertional 'indigestion' with sweating and weakness in an older adult is possible ACS until proven otherwise.
why: Older adults often describe cardiac ischemia as indigestion or weakness. Onset during exertion, heavy sweating, and borderline vital signs make this time-critical.
wrong: Exertional upper abdominal discomfort with sweating and weakness may be ACS; an antacid is not appropriate EMT care here.
Exertion increases the heart's oxygen demand and can worsen ischemia.
Waiting treats a possible heart attack as if it were harmless and loses time.

stem: An 86-year-old nursing home resident with a urinary catheter is 'not herself today,' according to staff. Which findings support suspicion of sepsis? Select THREE.
opts: Temperature of 96.0°F (35.6°C)
New confusion compared with her usual baseline
Respiratory rate of 26
A history of high blood pressure
Blood pressure of 148/86
An old, healed surgical scar on her abdomen
key: Sepsis in older adults may show a low temperature, new confusion, and rapid breathing rather than fever.
why: A likely infection source (catheter) plus abnormal temperature, altered mental status, and a fast respiratory rate point toward sepsis. Older adults often do not mount a fever.
wrong: Chronic high blood pressure is not a sign of infection or sepsis.
A normal-to-high BP does not support sepsis, though it also does not rule it out.
A healed scar is not a current source of infection.

stem: A 70-year-old man has had painful urination and chills for 3 days. Today he is confused. His skin is hot and flushed. HR 116, BP 90/56, RR 26, SpO2 95%, temperature 102.4°F. What should you do?
opts: Recognize likely sepsis, transport promptly, and alert the hospital
Transport non-emergently, since his oxygen saturation of 95% is normal
Encourage oral fluids and recommend he see his doctor tomorrow
Delay transport until his family can bring a medication list
key: Infection plus confusion, rapid breathing, and low BP suggests sepsis, a time-critical condition needing early notification.
why: Sepsis outcomes depend on early hospital treatment. Alerting the receiving facility lets them prepare antibiotics and fluids on arrival.
wrong: Normal SpO2 does not exclude sepsis; his low BP, tachycardia, and confusion make this time-critical.
He has signs of septic shock; delaying hospital care increases the risk of death.
A medication list is helpful but must not delay transport of a time-critical patient.

stem: A 28-year-old woman was ejected from a vehicle. She responds only to pain, her abdomen is rigid, and she is pale and cool. HR 132, BP 84/52. You have controlled her external bleeding and her airway is managed. The trauma center is 15 minutes away. What is the best plan?
opts: Complete a full head-to-toe exam on scene before moving her
Splint each suspected extremity fracture before loading
Load and transport now, continuing assessment and care en route
Wait on scene for ALS to arrive before transporting
key: A trauma patient in shock needs minimal on-scene time; begin transport and treat en route.
why: She likely has internal bleeding that only surgery can stop. Every minute on scene delays definitive care, so further assessment and treatment happen in the ambulance.
wrong: A detailed exam on scene delays definitive care; it can be done en route if time allows.
Detailed splinting delays transport in a patient in shock; it can be done en route if time allows.
Waiting for ALS delays surgical care; ALS can meet you en route if available.

stem: You are treating a 60-year-old man with chest pain who becomes pale and confused, with BP 80/50. ALS is 15 minutes from your location, and the nearest appropriate hospital is 10 minutes away. What is the best plan?
opts: Stay on scene and wait for ALS, since he needs advanced care
Begin transport now and arrange an ALS intercept per protocol
Stay on scene until his blood pressure improves
Request a helicopter and wait on scene for it to land
key: Do not wait on scene for ALS when it would delay hospital arrival; transport and coordinate an intercept per protocol.
why: The hospital can be reached sooner than ALS can arrive. Starting transport gets him to definitive care fastest, and an intercept en route can add ALS care if it helps.
wrong: Waiting 15 minutes on scene when the hospital is 10 minutes away delays definitive care.
His blood pressure will not improve on its own; waiting wastes time.
Waiting for an aircraft takes longer than ground transport to a hospital 10 minutes away.

stem: During a busy shift you assess four patients at separate calls. Which one is a high-priority patient who needs prompt transport?
opts: A 30-year-old with an isolated swollen ankle and a strong pedal pulse
A 45-year-old with a minor forearm laceration controlled by a dressing
A 22-year-old with a sore throat and mild fever and normal vital signs
A 58-year-old with chest pain, pale sweaty skin, and BP 86/54
key: Chest pain with signs of poor perfusion (shock) makes a patient high priority.
why: Chest pain with hypotension and pale, sweaty skin suggests a cardiac emergency with shock. The other patients have stable, non-life-threatening problems.
wrong: An isolated ankle injury with good circulation is low priority.
A minor laceration with controlled bleeding is low priority.
A sore throat with mild fever and normal vital signs is not time-critical.

stem: A 79-year-old woman tripped over a rug at home and struck her head on a table. She is alert and oriented, with a small scalp bruise and no other injuries. She takes apixaban, a blood thinner. Her vital signs are normal. Which statement best guides your decision?
opts: She can safely remain home because she is alert with normal vital signs
Only patients who lose consciousness need transport after a head strike
Transport is needed only if she develops a headache within the next hour
Her age and anticoagulant raise bleed risk; transport per triage guidelines
key: Anticoagulant use and a low-level fall with head impact at age 65+ are 2021 field triage risk factors: transport.
why: Older adults on anticoagulants can bleed inside the skull after minor falls and may look well at first. The 2021 field triage guideline lists anticoagulant use and low-level falls with significant head impact in adults 65 and older as risk factors for EMS judgment; she needs transport and evaluation at an appropriate facility.
wrong: Alertness and normal vital signs are common early in an intracranial bleed, especially in anticoagulated older adults.
Loss of consciousness is not required; anticoagulant use is a risk factor the 2021 field triage guideline asks EMS to weigh.
Symptoms of a brain bleed can appear hours later; waiting an hour does not make her safe to stay home.

stem: A family of four complains of headaches and nausea after running a generator in a closed garage during a power outage. You have moved everyone outdoors. The 40-year-old father is drowsy. HR 104, BP 138/84, RR 20, SpO2 99%. How should you interpret the pulse oximeter reading?
opts: It confirms adequate oxygenation, so oxygen is not needed
It suggests the headaches are from the stress of the outage
It may be falsely normal because carbon monoxide reads as oxygen
It is accurate as long as the waveform is strong and steady
key: Standard pulse oximetry can read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning; trust the history and symptoms.
why: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and standard oximeters read it as oxygenated hemoglobin. Several people with the same symptoms near a generator point to CO poisoning, which is treated with high-flow oxygen.
wrong: Standard oximeters read carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin as oxygenated, so a high value cannot be trusted; give high-flow oxygen.
Several people with the same symptoms in a space with a generator points to CO poisoning, not stress.
A good waveform reflects pulse detection, not whether hemoglobin carries oxygen or carbon monoxide.

stem: A 62-year-old man rescued from a cold lake is shivering hard, and his fingers are white and cold. HR 104, RR 18. The pulse oximeter shows a weak waveform reading 82%, yet he is talking in full sentences and his lips are pink. Which factors are most likely making this reading inaccurate? Select TWO.
opts: Poor blood flow to his cold fingers
Shivering that moves the probe
His heart rate of 104 beats per minute
His age, which is over 60 years
The fact that he is lying supine on the stretcher
key: Poor peripheral perfusion and motion cause unreliable SpO2 readings; compare the number with the patient's condition.
why: The oximeter needs a good pulse signal at the probe site. Cold, vasoconstricted fingers and shaking both degrade the signal, so the reading must be weighed against how the patient looks.
wrong: A moderately fast heart rate does not by itself cause an inaccurate reading.
Age alone does not make pulse oximetry inaccurate.
Lying supine does not affect the accuracy of the probe.

stem: Police ask you to evaluate a 50-year-old man found slumped in his car outside a bar. He smells of alcohol, is confused, and his speech is slurred. He is sweaty. HR 102, BP 136/82, RR 16, SpO2 97%. What assessment is most important to perform next?
opts: A field sobriety test with the officers
A blood glucose reading with a glucometer
A detailed medication history from his phone
An orthostatic blood pressure check
key: Check blood glucose in any patient with altered mental status; hypoglycemia can mimic intoxication.
why: Low blood sugar causes confusion, slurred speech, and sweating that look like drunkenness. A glucometer reading quickly identifies a reversible cause that the smell of alcohol could hide.
wrong: Sobriety testing is a police function and does not identify medical causes of altered mental status.
Medication history is useful later, but a quick glucose reading can identify a reversible cause now.
Orthostatic testing in a confused patient risks a fall and does not explain his altered mental status.

stem: A 63-year-old man with diabetes developed right-sided weakness and slurred speech 30 minutes ago. He is awake, follows commands, and swallows without difficulty. Glucometer reading is 42 mg/dL. HR 96, BP 152/90. What should you do?
opts: Give oral glucose per protocol, reassess neuro findings, and transport
Ignore the glucose reading because his symptoms clearly indicate a stroke
Withhold glucose because sugar can worsen brain injury in stroke
Give oral glucose and cancel transport if his weakness resolves
key: Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke; a glucometer reading is a key diagnostic test in any stroke-like presentation.
why: Low blood sugar can cause one-sided weakness and slurred speech. Because he can swallow, oral glucose is appropriate, followed by reassessment and transport, since a true stroke may still be present.
wrong: Hypoglycemia can cause one-sided weakness and slurred speech that mimics stroke; the low reading must be treated.
With a confirmed low reading, correcting hypoglycemia is the priority; untreated hypoglycemia itself injures the brain.
Even if symptoms resolve, he still needs transport and evaluation; a stroke may coexist.

stem: A 35-year-old man struck his head in a fall from a ladder. Over 20 minutes your vital signs are: BP 132/80, then 158/84, then 184/88; HR 88, then 70, then 54. His breathing is becoming irregular, and he is less responsive. What does this trend most likely indicate?
opts: Pain from his injuries driving up his blood pressure
Hypovolemic shock from hidden internal bleeding
A vasovagal reaction to the stress of the injury
Rising pressure inside the skull from brain injury
key: Rising BP, falling HR, and irregular breathing after head injury (Cushing's triad) suggest rising intracranial pressure.
why: As pressure inside the skull rises, the body raises blood pressure to keep blood flowing to the brain, and the heart slows in response. With declining responsiveness, this is a late, ominous trend.
wrong: Pain raises both BP and heart rate; it does not slow the pulse and cause irregular breathing.
Hypovolemic shock causes a rising heart rate and falling blood pressure, the opposite of this trend.
A vasovagal reaction lowers blood pressure rather than raising it.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has a closed femur fracture after a motorcycle crash. Your vital signs every 5 minutes are: HR 92, then 108, then 124; BP 128/80, then 126/82, then 124/80. Her skin is becoming pale and cool. What is the best interpretation?
opts: She is stable because her blood pressure has not changed
The rising heart rate is from pain and can be disregarded
She is likely developing shock from blood loss into the thigh
The readings are inconsistent, so trending them is not useful
key: A rising heart rate trend with cooling skin, even with a stable BP, signals developing shock.
why: A femur fracture can bleed heavily into the thigh. Blood pressure holds until late, so the steady rise in heart rate and the change in skin are the early warning.
wrong: Blood pressure is maintained until late; a steadily rising pulse with cooling skin shows worsening compensation.
Pain can raise heart rate, but a steady climb with pale, cool skin points to blood loss.
The trend is consistent and meaningful; repeated vital signs are how early deterioration is detected.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has been vomiting for 2 days and cannot keep fluids down. Lying down, her HR is 88 and BP 118/76. After she sits up for 1 minute, her HR is 118 and BP 98/64, and she feels lightheaded and nearly faints. What do these findings suggest?
opts: Significant fluid loss (volume depletion)
Normal changes expected when anyone sits up
Anxiety about having her vital signs taken
An inner-ear problem as the cause of all her symptoms
key: A marked rise in HR and fall in BP with lightheadedness on sitting or standing indicates volume depletion.
why: With low blood volume, the body cannot maintain blood pressure when the patient sits up, so the heart rate jumps and she becomes lightheaded. Two days of vomiting explain the fluid loss.
wrong: A healthy person's heart rate rises only slightly on sitting up; a 30-beat rise with a 20-point BP drop and near-fainting is abnormal.
Anxiety does not explain a postural BP drop with near-fainting after days of vomiting.
An inner-ear problem causes vertigo but not a postural fall in BP with a large rise in heart rate.

stem: A 72-year-old man felt lightheaded after several days of diarrhea. He is alert, has no trauma, and shows no signs of shock while lying down. Medical direction asks you to obtain orthostatic vital signs. Put the steps in the correct order.
opts: Have the patient lie supine and rest for a few minutes
Measure pulse and blood pressure while he is supine
Assist him to sit or stand, staying ready to support him
After 1 to 3 minutes, remeasure pulse and blood pressure
key: Orthostatic vital signs compare resting supine values with values taken within about 1 to 3 minutes of sitting or standing.
why: A resting supine baseline is needed for comparison. Rechecking after the position change shows whether the body can maintain blood pressure, and staying close prevents a fall if he becomes faint.
